passage:
Mentor note, Jaya.

Gautam came to my office at 8:30, hood up, eyes down. Someone had taken a photo at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth, and turned it into a meme going round three class groups. Gautam said very quietly, "Everyone's seen it. I want to disappear." Gautam hadn't eaten breakfast.

I told Gautam plainly that the cruelty belongs to the people making the meme, not to Gautam. I stayed while we reported the posts and blocked the accounts, and I passed the matter to the college's student welfare lead that same morning. Two friends from Gautam's hostel wing offered to walk with Gautam to lunch.

I reminded Gautam that these things fade faster than they feel today. I will check in tomorrow.

qa.a: The photo was taken at the farewell, catching Gautam mid-laugh with an open mouth.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when saying "I want to disappear"?
qa.a: Deep shame and exposure, shown by the hood up, the eyes down, the skipped breakfast and the wish to disappear.

qa.q: What did Jaya do, and what else could help?
qa.a: Jaya stayed with Gautam, reported the posts, blocked the accounts and told the welfare lead that morning; friends can keep walking with Gautam to meals and remind Gautam it fades.

qa.q: How might the two hostel friends' offer affect Gautam?
qa.a: Their offer to walk with Gautam to lunch shows the mockery is not everyone's view, which can make the shame feel less total.

grounding: People turn a photo of Gautam into a meme and shame flares, and the mentor helps report it, names the cruelty as the makers' and connects Gautam with friends.

passage:
Friday, 1:40 am

They made my photo into a meme. The one from Priya's sangeet where I'm mid-jump with my mouth open. Someone in the batch group added the words "when the fees are due" and now it's in four other groups. Omkar says it's even on a college page.

My face burned all through the lab. I kept thinking: I look ridiculous, I am ridiculous. I'm Arnab and I've never wanted to disappear so much.

Omkar sat with me after dinner. He said, "They're being cruel, you're not the joke." We reported the page together and I blocked the two guys who started it. Then he made me watch an old cricket match with him till I laughed at something else.

Last month's meme was about a professor's tie. Nobody remembers it now.

qa.q: Whose sangeet was the photo taken at?
qa.a: The photo was taken at Priya's sangeet.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling during the lab, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Arnab felt deep shame and humiliation; a burning face and the thought "I am ridiculous" show it.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that helped?
qa.a: Omkar named the cruelty as theirs, helped report the page and block the starters, and kept Arnab company with something ordinary.

qa.q: How does Omkar see the meme compared with how Arnab sees it?
qa.a: Omkar sees it as others being unkind that will fade like the tie meme, while Arnab first feels it as proof of being foolish.

grounding: The diary shows a young person humiliated by a meme who learns the cruelty belongs to others, reports, blocks and leans on a friend.

qa.q: How many shares did the post have?
What was Naveen feeling when wanting to delete the account?
qa.a: Naveen felt humiliated and ashamed, wanting to hide from everyone, and the racing heart shows how shaken Naveen was.

qa.q: How could a friend support someone in Naveen's place, as Neelam did?
qa.a: Say clearly it is the others' cruelty, help report and block right away, show up in person, and remind them memes fade fast.

qa.q: How might Naveen's cousin see the meme, and what would change if the cousin knew how Naveen felt?
qa.a: The cousin seems to see it as a harmless joke; knowing Naveen's hurt might make the cousin stop sharing and apologise.

grounding: The chat shows a young person mocked in a meme being reassured that it is others' cruelty, helped to report and block, and supported by a friend.
